name: Shri Vaijnath Temple (Vaidyanath Jyotirlinga)
style: Hemadpanthi
significance: A Shiva temple at Parli Vaijnath in Beed district counted as the fifth of the twelve Jyotirlingas, and among the most visited pilgrimage shrines of Marathwada.

name: Tulja Bhavani Temple
significance: A 12th-century temple to the goddess Bhavani, counted among the Shakta pithas and one of the three-and-a-half principal Shakti seats of Maharashtra. It is among the most heavily visited pilgrimage shrines in the state.
story: The Skanda Purana relates that the goddess came to the aid of the ascetic widow Anubhuti on Yamunachala hill and afterwards settled at Tuljapur as Tulja Bhavani.

name: Mahalakshmi Temple, Kolhapur
significance: A major goddess temple where Mahalakshmi is worshipped locally as Ambabai, reckoned one of the three-and-a-half Shakti seats of the Shakta tradition in Maharashtra.
story: The goddess is said to have manifested here to destroy the demon Kolhasur, from whom Kolhapur takes its name.

name: Renuka Devi Temple, Mahur
significance: A hill shrine to Renuka, mother of Parashurama, counted among the three-and-a-half Shakta pithas of Maharashtra; the surrounding town is also revered as the birthplace of Dattatreya.
story: Renuka was mortally wounded by Sahasrarjuna when she refused to surrender the cow Kamadhenu, and her son Parashurama performed her last rites at Mahur, where she then manifested on the hill.

name: Saptashrungi Temple
deity: Goddess Saptashrungi Nivasini (a form of Durga)
significance: A hill shrine where the goddess is carved into a cave in a sheer rock face, counted among Maharashtra's three-and-a-half Shakta pithas and among the wider set of 51 Shakta pithas.
story: The right arm of Sati is said to have fallen here as Shiva carried her body across the world.

name: Shani Shingnapur Temple
deity: Shani, worshipped as a swayambhu black stone
significance: An open-air shrine to Shani built around a self-manifested black stone. The surrounding village is known for houses and shops built without doors or locks, in the belief that the god himself punishes theft.
story: Shepherds are said to have struck a black stone that bled, after which Shani appeared in a shepherd's dream, claimed the stone as his own and promised the village protection from theft.

name: Khandoba Temple, Jejuri
deity: Khandoba (Malhari Martand, a form of Shiva)
style: Hemadpanthi
significance: One of the foremost pilgrimage centres of Maharashtra, this hilltop temple to Khandoba is the family deity shrine of farming, Brahmin and Dhangar communities across the Deccan.
story: Khandoba is said to have descended as an avatar of Shiva to subdue the demon brothers Mani and Malla, killing one and pardoning the other when he vowed to serve people.

name: Bhuleshwar Temple
significance: A hilltop Shiva temple about 45 km from Pune, protected as a monument and known for its dense figural stone carving worked in black basalt.
story: Devotees say that sweets offered before the linga sometimes disappear from the offering bowl.

name: Dagadusheth Halwai Ganapati Temple
significance: Pune's best-known Ganesha temple, visited by well over a hundred thousand devotees a year and the focus of a prominent ten-day Ganeshotsav celebration.
story: The sweet-seller Dagadusheth Halwai and his wife Laxmibai are said to have founded the shrine on a sage's advice after losing their only son in a plague.

name: Chintamani Temple, Theur
significance: One of the larger and better-known Ashtavinayaka shrines, about 25 km from Pune near the confluence of the Bhima and Mula-Mutha. It was a major Ganapatya centre that drew royal patronage under the Peshwa Madhavrao I.
story: Ganesha is said to have recovered the wish-granting Chintamani jewel from the greedy king Gana for the sage Kapila and then stayed on at Theur.

name: Mayureshwar (Moreshwar) Temple, Morgaon
builtDisplay: not earlier than 17th c.; Peshwa-era patronage
style: Nagara with Islamic-influenced corner minarets
significance: The starting and finishing point of the eight-temple Ashtavinayaka pilgrimage and the principal centre of the Ganapatya sect, enclosed by a tall stone wall with minarets at its corners.
story: Ganesha is said to have incarnated as Mayuresvara, riding a peacock, to defeat the demon Sindhu.

name: Siddhivinayak Temple, Siddhatek
style: black stone, north-facing sanctum under a domed ceiling
significance: The third of the eight Ashtavinayaka shrines and the only one in the Ahilyanagar (Ahmednagar) district; its image is unusual in having a right-turned trunk.
story: Vishnu is said to have performed penance here invoking Ganesha, receiving the siddhis with which he overcame the demons Madhu and Kaitabha.

name: Ballaleshwar Temple, Pali
style: east-facing stone temple laid out in the shape of the letter 'shri'
significance: One of the eight Ashtavinayaka shrines and the only Ganesha temple known by the name of a devotee rather than of the god.
story: A boy named Ballal worshipped a stone as Ganesha despite his father's beatings; the god appeared, healed him and agreed to remain there under the boy's name.

name: Varadvinayak Temple, Mahad
significance: One of the eight Ashtavinayaka shrines, in Mahad village of Khalapur taluka; the present temple was raised in 1725 by the Peshwa general Ramji Mahadev Biwalkar around an image reported found in 1690.
story: The sage Gritsamada's prayers are said to have won Ganesha's promise to dwell here permanently as Varadavinayaka, the granter of boons.

name: Girijatmaj Temple, Lenyadri
builtDisplay: 1st–3rd c. Buddhist cave, later given to Ganesha worship
style: rock-cut Buddhist vihara adapted as a Hindu shrine
significance: The only Ashtavinayaka shrine set on a mountain and inside a Buddhist cave group, occupying cells of Cave 7 of the Lenyadri excavations.
story: Parvati is said to have meditated here for twelve years, after which Ganesha granted that he would be born as her son.

name: Vigneshwara (Vighnahar) Temple, Ozar
deity: Ganesha as Vigneshwara, remover of obstacles
style: walled courtyard temple with a gold-foiled shikhara and lamp towers
significance: One of the eight Ashtavinayaka shrines, believed to house a self-existent image; it was renovated by Chimaji Appa after his capture of Vasai Fort and again in 1967.
story: Ganesha subdued the demon Vignasura, sent by Indra to wreck a king's sacrifice, and at the demon's request took the title Vigneshwara.

name: Mahaganapati Temple, Ranjangaon
significance: An east-facing Ashtavinayaka shrine whose main structure dates from the Peshwa period and was later renovated by Madhavrao I and Sardar Kibe of Indore.
story: The presiding image, gifted by the local Khollam family of goldsmiths, is described as having ten trunks and twenty arms.

name: Mumba Devi Temple
deity: Goddess Mumba, a local form of the mother goddess
builtDisplay: rebuilt at Bhuleshwar after 1739–1770; shrine about six centuries old
significance: The temple of the goddess from whom Mumbai takes its name, first built by Koli fishermen at Bori Bunder and re-established at Bhuleshwar after the original was destroyed in the mid-18th century.
story: Parvati is said to have taken birth as the fisherwoman Mumba among the Koli people, and to have stayed on as their village deity at their request.

name: Mahalakshmi Temple, Mumbai
significance: One of Mumbai's most visited temples, built in 1831 by the merchant Dhakji Dadaji and housing the three goddesses of the Tridevi.

name: Walkeshwar Temple
significance: An old Shiva temple on Malabar Hill in South Mumbai, associated with the adjoining Banganga freshwater tank and used as a venue for Hindustani classical music festivals.
story: Rama is said to have paused here on his way to Lanka, fashioning a linga of sand and shooting an arrow into the ground to bring up the Ganga as the Banganga tank.

name: Kanheri Caves
deity: Buddhist monastic complex of viharas and chaityas
style: rock-cut Buddhist architecture in basalt
significance: A group of 109 caves cut into a basalt outcrop inside Sanjay Gandhi National Park, forming a long-lived Buddhist monastic and teaching centre on the Konkan coast with elaborate water-management works.

name: Karla Caves
builtDisplay: 2nd c. BCE–5th c. CE; Great Chaitya c. 50–70 CE
style: rock-cut chaitya hall with apsidal plan and wooden roof ribs
significance: A rock-cut Buddhist cave complex near Lonavala containing the Great Chaitya, the largest rock-cut chaitya hall in India, funded by rulers, merchants and Yavana donors.

name: Bhaja Caves
builtDisplay: 2nd c. BCE, with inscriptions to the 2nd c. CE
style: rock-cut Buddhist architecture imitating timber construction
significance: A group of 22 rock-cut caves near Lonavala whose barrel-vaulted chaitya and reliefs document the early development of Buddhist architecture; one carving is cited as evidence that drums of the tabla type were in use over two millennia ago.

name: Global Vipassana Pagoda
deity: Vipassana meditation dome dedicated to the teaching of Sayagyi U Ba Khin
style: Burmese, modelled on the Shwedagon Pagoda
significance: A donation-funded meditation hall at Gorai seating roughly 8,000 practitioners beneath what is described as the world's largest stone dome built without supporting pillars; it was inaugurated in 2009 as a monument to Vipassana practice.

name: Deekshabhoomi
style: modelled on the Great Stupa at Sanchi
significance: The Nagpur site where B. R. Ambedkar and some 400,000 followers embraced Buddhism on 14 October 1956, the largest mass religious conversion on record; its hollow stupa is central to Ambedkarite Buddhism and draws millions of pilgrims.

name: Ganpatipule Temple
significance: A shrine on the Konkan shore in Ratnagiri district whose west-facing image, said to have risen from the soil, makes it one of coastal Maharashtra's busiest pilgrimage and tourist destinations.
story: Local tradition holds that Ganpati moved here from nearby Gule after taking offence at a villager's remark, the name Pule meaning that he came forward.

name: Shiv Mandir, Ambarnath (Ambreshwar Temple)
style: Bhumija
significance: An 11th-century Shilahara temple on the Waldhuni river near Mumbai, likely raised by King Chhittaraja. It is a well-known example of Bhumija architecture, with a sanctum set below floor level and a shikhara left unfinished.

name: Kopeshwar Temple
significance: A 12th-century Shiva temple on the bank of the Krishna, built under the Shilahara king Gandaraditya and known for its open Swargamandapa and dense carving; it is noted as a Shiva temple that also enshrines an image of Vishnu.
story: Vishnu is said to have brought Shiva here to calm his rage after Sati's death at Daksha's sacrifice, which is why the god is called Kopeshwar, the wrathful one.

name: Shri Gajanan Maharaj Sansthan, Shegaon
deity: Samadhi shrine of Sant Gajanan Maharaj
significance: The samadhi temple of the saint Gajanan Maharaj, who died in 1910, administered by a trust formed in 1908. It has made Shegaon one of the largest pilgrimage centres of Vidarbha, drawing hundreds of thousands of visitors a year.
story: A dhuni fire lit by the saint is said to have burned continuously beside his samadhi ever since.

name: Shree Swami Samarth Math, Akkalkot
deity: Samadhi shrine of Swami Samarth of Akkalkot
significance: The shrine of Swami Samarth, a 19th-century master of the Dattatreya tradition who came to Akkalkot around 1856 and took samadhi in 1878; his large following across Maharashtra keeps the ashram a busy pilgrimage centre.
story: The Swami said that he had emerged from a banyan tree and had earlier borne the name Nrusimha Bhan, and devotees regard him as an incarnation of Dattatreya.

name: Mangueshi Temple
deity: Shiva as Manguesh, worshipped as a linga
builtDisplay: linga moved here 1560; present structure Maratha era, renovated 1890 and 1973
style: Goan Saraswat, with a seven-storey deepastambha
significance: One of the largest and most visited temples in Goa and the family deity shrine of many Gaud Saraswat Brahmins; the linga was carried here from Kushasthali in 1560 to escape Portuguese conversions.
story: Shiva is said to have fled Kailash after losing at dice and to have taken the form of a tiger to frighten Parvati, whose cry of Mam Girisha became the name Manguesh.

name: Shanta Durga Temple
style: Goan Saraswat, with pyramidal shikhara and a balustraded dome
significance: A Goud Saraswat Brahmin temple about 30 km from Panaji, patronised by Baji Rao I in 1738 and serving as the family deity shrine for many Saraswat households.
story: Shantadurga is said to have stepped between Shiva and Vishnu in a destructive quarrel, holding one on each hand until peace was restored.

name: Mahalasa Narayani Temple, Mardol
deity: Mahalasa Narayani, a form of Vishnu as Mohini
significance: The chief temple of Mahalasa, a major pilgrimage centre in Ponda taluka and the family goddess shrine of Gaud Saraswat and Daivajnya Brahmin and Vaishnava households across Goa and the Konkan.
story: Folk tradition makes Mhalsa the daughter of the merchant Timmaseth, married to Khandoba at his command in a dream, at which two Shiva lingas are said to have appeared.

name: Mahadev Temple, Tambdi Surla
style: Kadamba, in basalt
significance: A 13th-century basalt temple deep in the forest of the Western Ghats, protected as a Monument of National Importance and the only well-preserved example of Kadamba temple architecture surviving in Goa.
story: Local tradition holds that a large king cobra lives permanently in the dim sanctum beside the linga.

name: Saptakoteshwar Temple
style: Kadamba plan with a shallow Mughal-style dome, European-style mandapa and a deepastamba
significance: One of the six great Shiva sites of the Konkan and the family deity shrine of the Kadamba kings; the present structure was commissioned by Shivaji in 1668 after the linga had been rescued and moved during Portuguese rule.
story: The Skanda Purana relates that seven sages made a linga of seven metals here, and that Shiva agreed to remain as Saptakoteshwar, lord of the seven.

name: Bhojeshwar Temple
style: Bhumija/Latina, planned as a svargarohana-prasada
significance: An unfinished 11th-century Shiva temple attributed to the Paramara king Bhoja, housing a 7.5-foot linga. Because work stopped, the site preserves architectural drawings, mason marks and quarry remains that document medieval temple construction in unusual detail.
story: Merutunga's Prabandha-Chintamani has King Bhoja describing to the poet Magha the Bhojasvamin temple he intended to raise in Malwa, though the two men lived centuries apart.

name: Sharda Devi Temple, Maihar
significance: A hilltop temple on Trikut hill counted among the Shakti Pithas and one of the busiest goddess shrines of Madhya Pradesh, especially during Navaratri.
story: Sati's necklace is said to have fallen here, giving Maihar its name, and the warriors Alha and Udal are remembered as the first to worship the goddess in the forest.

name: Pitambara Peeth
deity: Goddess Bagalamukhi, one of the ten Mahavidyas
significance: A temple complex and ashram at Datia founded in the 1920s by Shree Swami Ji, among the best known shrines of Bagalamukhi, with further temples to Dhumavati, Parashurama, Hanuman and Kal Bhairav and a Sanskrit library.
story: The Vankhandeswar linga within the complex is held by tradition to date from the time of the Mahabharata.

name: Bijasan Mata Temple, Salkanpur
deity: Bijasan Devi (Vindhyavasini, a form of Durga)
significance: A Siddhapeeth of Vindhyavasini Bijasan Devi standing about 800 feet above the plain near Rehti in Sehore district, and one of the most frequented goddess shrines in Madhya Pradesh.

name: Ram Raja Temple
deity: Rama, worshipped as a reigning king
significance: The only temple where Rama is worshipped as a king, and in a palace rather than a purpose-built shrine; it was established by Madhukar Shah of Orchha and his queen and receives hundreds of thousands of visitors a year.
story: Queen Ganesh Kunwari is said to have received the child Rama in her lap at the Sarayu in Ayodhya and to have brought him to Orchha on three conditions, after which the image refused to be moved from her palace.

name: Chaturbhuj Temple, Orchha
deity: Vishnu; intended for Rama and now serving Radha Krishna
style: Nagara with Maru-Gurjara elements, combining temple, fort and palace forms
significance: A towering Bundela temple at Orchha with one of the tallest vimanas of any Indian temple, begun by Madhukar Shah and completed by his son Vir Singh Deo during Akbar's reign.
story: It was raised for the Rama image the queen brought from Ayodhya, but the image would not be moved from her palace, which became the Ram Raja temple instead.

name: Chausath Yogini Temple, Mitaoli
deity: The 64 Yoginis, with Shiva in the central shrine
style: circular hypaethral yogini temple with 65 chambers
significance: An 11th-century circular yogini temple, also called the Ekattarso Mahadeva temple, built under King Devapala and protected by the ASI; its ring plan is often cited as an inspiration for the design of India's parliament building.
story: The yoginis were believed able to fly, which is given as the reason the central courtyard is left open to the sky.

name: Bateshwar Hindu Temples
style: post-Gupta and early Gurjara-Pratihara North Indian, including mandapika shrines
significance: A group of nearly 200 sandstone temples and ruins spread over about 25 acres north of Gwalior, forming an unusually dense record of experimentation in early medieval temple design in central India.

name: Kakanmath Temple
style: North Indian, with a shikhara about 30 m high
significance: A ruined 11th-century Shiva temple at Sihoniya commissioned by the Kachchhapaghata ruler Kirttiraja, now a Monument of National Importance under the ASI.
story: The name is popularly explained as honouring Kakanavati, said to have been the queen of one Surajpala.

name: Udayagiri Caves
deity: Vishnu and Shiva, with one cave dedicated to the Jain tirthankara Parshvanatha
builtDisplay: early 3rd–5th c.; principal caves consecrated 401 CE
style: early Gupta rock-cut architecture
significance: A hillside of rock-cut sanctuaries near Vidisha holding some of the oldest surviving Hindu temple architecture and iconography in India, including the great Varaha panel, and the only Gupta site with securely dated royal inscriptions.
story: The Varaha panel shows Vishnu in boar form lifting the earth goddess Bhudevi clear of the demon Hiranyaksha.

name: Chausath Yogini Temple, Bhedaghat (Golaki Math)
deity: Eighty-one yoginis around a central Shiva-Bhairava shrine
style: circular yogini temple about 125 ft across with 81 cells
significance: The largest of the circular yogini temples, set on a hilltop above the Narmada near Jabalpur and built under Yuvaraja II of the Kalachuris; unusually it holds 81 shrine cells rather than the customary 64.
